stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 28 year old G2P0 with 6 weeks and 5 days amenorrhoea and 2 days of light per vaginum bleeding without pain. She has one previous first trimester miscarriage and no other medical history. She has an IUD in situ for contraception which is visible on speculum and she is happy to attend for repeat blood tests every 3 to 4 days if needed.

On examination she is haemodynamically stable and non-tender. Vital signs: pulse 78/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius. Serum beta hCG today is 2400 IU/L, up from 1900 IU/L 48 hours ago. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus, a 22 mm right adnexal mass with no yolk sac and no foetal cardiac activity, and no free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Serum creatinine, ALT, and full blood count are within normal limits.

data_table.Vitals: HR 78; BP 118/72; RR 14; SpO2 99 percent; T 36.7
data_table.Serum bhCG: 2400 IU/L today; 1900 IU/L 48 hours ago (suboptimal rise)
data_table.Transvaginal ultrasound: Empty uterus; right adnexal mass 22 mm; no yolk sac; no foetal cardiac activity; no free fluid
data_table.Laboratory: Creatinine, ALT, and FBC within normal limits
data_table.Social factors: Reliable follow-up available; IUD in situ

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management option to offer?

options.text: Uterine evacuation with suction curettage to obtain products for histological diagnosis in the theatre
options.rationale: Diagnostic curettage is not standard in AU practice for ectopic diagnosis, delays treatment, and risks removing a coexisting intrauterine pregnancy; ultrasound and serial bhCG give the diagnosis without curettage (Source: RANZCOG GPS Management of Ectopic Pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG GPS Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Single-dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2 with serial bhCG on days 4 and 7 in reliable follow-up
options.rationale: This ectopic meets RANZCOG criteria for medical management: stable haemodynamics, bhCG under 5000 IU/L, mass under 3.5 cm, no foetal cardiac activity, no significant pain or free fluid, reliable follow-up, and no medical contraindication to methotrexate; single-dose methotrexate 50 mg/m2 with days 4 and 7 bhCG is the standard (Source: RANZCOG GPS Management of Ectopic Pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG GPS Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Two-dose methotrexate 50 mg/m2 on days 0 and 4 without checking a follow-up day 7 bhCG level
options.rationale: Single-dose protocol is the default in Australian practice with days 4 and 7 bhCG monitoring; multi-dose regimens are reserved for higher initial bhCG or persistent trophoblast after single dose (Source: RANZCOG GPS Management of Ectopic Pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG GPS Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Expectant management with weekly bhCG measurements and clinical review, no pharmacological intervention
options.rationale: Expectant management is limited to a decreasing bhCG under 1500 IU/L with a small mass and no symptoms; this bhCG is rising and above 1500, so medical or surgical management is required (Source: RANZCOG GPS Management of Ectopic Pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG GPS Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Emergency laparoscopic salpingectomy without prior consent for medical management as first-line treatment
options.rationale: Surgery is indicated when medical criteria are not met (bhCG 5000 IU/L or above, mass 3.5 cm or above, foetal cardiac activity, haemodynamic instability, severe pain, free fluid, unreliable follow-up); this patient meets medical criteria (Source: RANZCOG GPS Management of Ectopic Pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG GPS Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

explanation.summary: Medical management of tubal ectopic pregnancy with methotrexate 50 mg/m2 intramuscular is acceptable when bhCG is under 5000 IU/L, adnexal mass is under 3.5 cm, no foetal cardiac activity is seen, the patient is haemodynamically stable with no significant pain or haemoperitoneum, follow-up is reliable, and there is no contraindication to methotrexate (bloods normal, no breastfeeding, no immunodeficiency). Follow-up bhCG on days 4 and 7 checks for a 15 percent drop; failure triggers a second methotrexate dose or surgery. Expectant management is limited to falling bhCG under 1500 IU/L.
key_points: Methotrexate criteria: bhCG <5000, mass <3.5 cm, no cardiac activity, stable, reliable follow-up
Single dose 50 mg/m2 with days 4 and 7 bhCG in AU practice
Surgery when medical criteria not met or bhCG fails to fall by 15 percent day 4 to 7
explanation.pearls: The bhCG threshold that flips ectopic to surgical management is 5000 IU/L, not 3000; a doubling reference range does not apply once ectopic is diagnosed.

sources.label: RANZCOG GPS Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 34 year old G2P2 woman at her 6 week postnatal review. She is exclusively breastfeeding her healthy term baby every 2 to 3 hours. Her only medical history is migraine without aura for the last 5 years. Her BMI today is 27 kg/m2 and her blood pressure is 118/76 mmHg. She would like reliable contraception but wants to protect her breastmilk supply and preserve the option of another pregnancy in about 3 years.

She had an uncomplicated vaginal birth without perineal trauma. She is not currently amenorrhoeic as she had a small amount of vaginal bleeding 10 days ago. She is comfortable with an intrauterine device and has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism.

data_table.Postnatal history: G2P2, 6 weeks postpartum; uncomplicated vaginal birth; exclusive breastfeeding 2 to 3 hourly
data_table.Medical background: Migraine without aura; BMI 27; BP 118/76; no VTE history
data_table.Fertility plan: Desires reliable contraception now; another pregnancy in about 3 years
data_table.Bleeding pattern: Vaginal bleeding 10 days ago; not amenorrhoeic

lead_in: What is the most appropriate contraceptive to recommend?

options.text: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg intramuscular every 12 weeks for the next 3 years
options.rationale: Depot medroxyprogesterone can delay return to fertility for up to 12 months after cessation, which does not fit a plan to conceive in about 3 years and is less reversible than an IUD or implant (Source: eTG Contraception).
source_refs: eTG Contraception

options.text: Etonogestrel subdermal implant with combined oral contraception as backup for the first month
options.rationale: The implant is a reasonable option but combined oral contraception as backup would not be added because combined hormones are avoided in breastfeeding until at least 6 weeks; the recommendation should not include CHC (Source: eTG Contraception).
source_refs: eTG Contraception

options.text: Rely on lactational amenorrhoea method alone as her primary contraception for the next 6 months
options.rationale: LAM requires exclusive breastfeeding, amenorrhoea, and an infant under 6 months; this patient is not amenorrhoeic which invalidates LAM as her primary method (Source: eTG Contraception).
source_refs: eTG Contraception

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill 30 microgram ethinyloestradiol plus levonorgestrel 150 microgram daily
options.rationale: Combined hormonal contraception is avoided until at least 6 weeks postpartum in breastfeeding women because of small effects on milk supply and higher VTE risk in the puerperium (Source: eTG Contraception).
source_refs: eTG Contraception

options.text: Insertion of the 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine device today with contraception effective immediately
options.rationale: The 52 mg LNG-IUD is a long-acting reversible contraceptive with no impact on breastfeeding, works well in the postpartum period, and provides highly effective contraception aligned with her 3 year plan; insertion at 4 weeks postpartum or later is appropriate (Source: eTG Contraception).
source_refs: eTG Contraception

explanation.summary: For a breastfeeding woman at 6 weeks postpartum wanting reliable contraception with rapid reversibility, the LNG-IUD (52 mg) is the highest tier long-acting reversible option and does not affect milk supply. Combined hormonal contraception is deferred until at least 6 weeks postpartum in breastfeeding women because of small milk supply effects and higher puerperal VTE risk. LAM requires exclusive breastfeeding, amenorrhoea, and infant under 6 months. Depot medroxyprogesterone has a documented delay in fertility return of up to 12 months, which does not suit a woman planning pregnancy in 3 years.
key_points: LNG-IUD at 4 weeks or later is safe in breastfeeding and gives immediate reliable contraception
Combined hormonal contraception deferred until at least 6 weeks postpartum in breastfeeding women
Depot medroxyprogesterone can delay fertility return by up to 12 months
explanation.pearls: Migraine with aura contraindicates combined hormonal contraception; migraine without aura is a stricter risk to weigh alongside age and vascular risk factors.

subtopic_detail: Tocolysis choice with contraindication to first-line agent
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a tertiary maternity unit assessing a 27 year old G3P1 woman at 30 weeks and 2 days gestation presenting with regular painful uterine tightenings every 4 minutes for 3 hours. She has a history of severe migraine treated with regular propranolol and a normal echocardiogram in her first pregnancy. Antenatal course this pregnancy has been unremarkable and she has had no antepartum haemorrhage.

Vaginal examination is 2 cm dilated and 70 percent effaced with the cephalic vertex at station minus 2. Membranes are intact. The cardiotocograph is reassuring with a baseline of 140/min and moderate variability. Vital signs: pulse 88/min, blood pressure 108/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99 percent, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius. Foetal fibronectin is positive and a transvaginal cervical length is 18 mm. Betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular has been given and magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenous loading dose is running for neuroprotection.

data_table.Gestation and history: G3P1 at 30+2; regular contractions every 4 minutes; propranolol for migraine
data_table.Examination: 2 cm dilated, 70 percent effaced, station -2; membranes intact
data_table.Ultrasound and biomarker: Cervical length 18 mm; foetal fibronectin positive
data_table.Vital signs: HR 88; BP 108/62; RR 18; SpO2 99 percent; T 36.9
data_table.Given so far: Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM x1; magnesium sulfate 4 g IV loading for neuroprotection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate tocolytic to commence?

options.text: Intravenous atosiban 6.75 mg bolus then 300 microgram/min infusion tapered over 48 hours
options.rationale: Atosiban is not available on the PBS in Australia and is not the first-line tocolytic here; nifedipine gives comparable efficacy at lower cost and is preferred (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 62 Preterm Labour and Birth).
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 62 Preterm Labour and Birth

options.text: Intravenous salbutamol infusion titrated to fewer than one contraction in 10 minutes as tocolysis
options.rationale: Salbutamol is contraindicated in a woman on propranolol because the pharmacological antagonism causes unpredictable bronchospasm and cardiovascular effects; salbutamol is no longer preferred for tocolysis in AU because of maternal cardiovascular events (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 62 Preterm Labour and Birth).
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 62 Preterm Labour and Birth

options.text: Oral indomethacin 100 mg loading dose then 25 to 50 mg every 6 hours for a total of 48 hours
options.rationale: Indomethacin is avoided after 32 weeks because of premature closure of the ductus arteriosus and oligohydramnios; at 30+2 the risk is smaller but still concerning and nifedipine is the safer first-line at this gestation (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 62 Preterm Labour and Birth).
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 62 Preterm Labour and Birth

options.text: Continue the magnesium sulfate infusion at a higher rate for both neuroprotection and tocolysis
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate at neuroprotective doses does not provide effective tocolysis; using it for tocolysis has been associated with paediatric mortality signals and is not RANZCOG's tocolytic of choice (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 62 Preterm Labour and Birth).
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 62 Preterm Labour and Birth

options.text: Oral nifedipine 20 mg loading dose then 10 to 20 mg every 6 to 8 hours titrated to contractions
options.rationale: Nifedipine is the RANZCOG first-line tocolytic for women under 34 weeks needing 48 hours of steroid cover; salbutamol is contraindicated because she takes propranolol (beta-blocker interaction risks bronchospasm and haemodynamic instability), and indomethacin is avoided at 30 weeks because of ductus arteriosus constriction risk (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 62 Preterm Labour and Birth).
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 62 Preterm Labour and Birth

explanation.summary: Tocolysis under 34 weeks buys 48 hours for corticosteroid maturation and inutero transfer, not to prolong pregnancy indefinitely. RANZCOG places nifedipine first because of efficacy, oral route, and safety profile. Beta-agonists such as salbutamol are largely displaced from AU practice because of maternal cardiovascular events, and concurrent propranolol adds a further relative contraindication. Indomethacin is avoided beyond 32 weeks and used with caution before; magnesium sulfate is a neuroprotective agent, not a tocolytic, and atosiban is not funded on the PBS.
key_points: Nifedipine first-line tocolytic in AU practice under 34 weeks
Salbutamol contraindicated with concurrent beta-blocker and largely deprecated in AU
Indomethacin avoided beyond 32 weeks because of ductus arteriosus constriction
explanation.pearls: Concurrent beta-blocker use flips tocolysis choice away from beta-agonists; check the maternal medication list before drawing up any uterine relaxant.

sources.label: RANZCOG C-Obs 62 Preterm Labour and Birth

subtopic_detail: Antihypertensive selection during severe pre-eclampsia with contraindication to first-line
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 30 year old primigravida at 33 weeks gestation with new onset severe hypertension. She has known moderate asthma with a hospital admission last year and uses a fluticasone-salmeterol preventer daily. She has no other medical history and no known drug allergies. Antenatal care has been shared care through her GP.

Blood pressure on repeat measurements is 172/112 mmHg and 170/108 mmHg 15 minutes apart. She reports a moderate frontal headache but no visual disturbance and no epigastric pain. Reflexes are brisk without clonus. Vital signs: pulse 96/min, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 98 percent, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. Investigations: urinary protein-creatinine ratio 68 mg/mmol, platelets 128 x 10^9/L (150 to 400), ALT 62 U/L (under 40), creatinine 78 micromol/L (45 to 90), uric acid 0.42 mmol/L. The cardiotocograph is reassuring.

data_table.Symptoms: Frontal headache; no visual disturbance; no epigastric pain
data_table.Bloods: Platelets 128; ALT 62; creatinine 78; uric acid 0.42; urinary PCR 68
data_table.Medication background: Moderate asthma on fluticasone-salmeterol; hospital admission for asthma last year

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line antihypertensive to give now?

options.text: Sublingual glyceryl trinitrate spray 400 microgram every 5 minutes until the blood pressure falls
options.rationale: Sublingual GTN is not a SOMANZ first-line antihypertensive for pre-eclampsia; it lacks safety data in pregnancy for this indication and can cause abrupt drops in blood pressure with foetal compromise (Source: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy).
source_refs: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy

options.text: Oral labetalol 200 mg with a repeat dose in 30 minutes as first-line acute antihypertensive therapy
options.rationale: Labetalol has beta-blocking activity which is relatively contraindicated in moderate to severe asthma; nifedipine is preferred here even though labetalol is otherwise first-line in SOMANZ (Source: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy).
source_refs: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy

options.text: Oral methyldopa 500 mg loading dose then 250 to 500 mg three times daily as first-line acute therapy
options.rationale: Methyldopa is an oral maintenance drug for chronic hypertension in pregnancy but is too slow to work for acute severe hypertension where blood pressure must fall within an hour (Source: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy).
source_refs: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy

options.text: Oral nifedipine immediate-release 10 mg with a repeat dose every 30 minutes as clinically required
options.rationale: SOMANZ preferred first-line antihypertensives for severe hypertension in pregnancy are oral labetalol, oral nifedipine immediate-release, or intravenous hydralazine; oral labetalol is relatively contraindicated in moderate to severe asthma so nifedipine becomes the preferred oral option (Source: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy).
source_refs: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose alone to lower blood pressure and prevent eclampsia
options.rationale: Magnesium is a neuroprotective anticonvulsant, not an antihypertensive; failing to give a specific antihypertensive leaves severe hypertension untreated with stroke risk (Source: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy).
source_refs: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy

explanation.summary: Severe hypertension in pregnancy (systolic 170 mmHg or above, or diastolic 110 mmHg or above) is a clinical emergency and blood pressure must be controlled within about an hour to lower stroke risk. SOMANZ lists oral labetalol, oral nifedipine immediate-release, and intravenous hydralazine as first-line acute options, with magnesium sulfate for eclampsia prophylaxis in parallel. In moderate to severe asthma the beta-blocking activity of labetalol makes it relatively contraindicated, so nifedipine (or intravenous hydralazine if oral is impractical) becomes first-line. Methyldopa is oral maintenance therapy, not an acute agent.
key_points: SOMANZ severe hypertension: oral labetalol, oral nifedipine IR, or IV hydralazine as first-line
Labetalol relatively contraindicated in moderate to severe asthma
Methyldopa is maintenance, not acute; magnesium is anticonvulsant, not antihypertensive
explanation.pearls: Comorbid asthma is the most common reason to pick nifedipine over labetalol; the systemic beta-blocking dose in oral labetalol is enough to trigger bronchospasm in an asthmatic.

sources.label: SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Vasa praevia recognition and delivery timing
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 29 year old primigravida at 34 weeks gestation who has just experienced a sudden painless per vaginum blood loss of about 30 mL immediately after spontaneous rupture of membranes at home. She has an in-vitro fertilisation twin pregnancy with a bilobed placenta noted on her 20 week morphology scan and a velamentous cord insertion of the leading twin identified on Doppler ultrasound at 24 weeks.

On arrival she is not in labour. Vital signs: pulse 92/min, blood pressure 110/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 99 percent, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius. Twin 1 cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 100/min falling to 80/min with recurrent variable decelerations; twin 2 baseline is 138/min with moderate variability and no decelerations. Speculum examination confirms membranes have ruptured and there is fresh red blood in the vagina without cervical dilatation.

data_table.Gestation and pregnancy: IVF twin pregnancy at 34 weeks; bilobed placenta; velamentous cord insertion of leading twin at 24 weeks
data_table.Presenting event: Sudden painless PV bleed of about 30 mL immediately after SROM
data_table.Twin 1 CTG: Baseline 100/min falling to 80/min with recurrent variable decelerations
data_table.Maternal vitals: HR 92; BP 110/68; RR 20; SpO2 99 percent; T 36.7

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continuous cardiotocograph monitoring for 4 hours with expectant management if maternal bleeding stops
options.rationale: Expectant management is unsafe once foetal decelerations and painless PV bleeding follow SROM in a woman with a known velamentous cord; foetal exsanguination is minutes not hours (Source: RANZCOG GPS Vasa Praevia).
source_refs: RANZCOG GPS Vasa Praevia

options.text: Insertion of a large-bore intravenous cannula and cross-match 4 maternal red cell units before deciding on delivery
options.rationale: Maternal transfusion cannot rescue foetal exsanguination in vasa praevia; ordering cross-match delays the only intervention that saves the foetus, which is immediate delivery (Source: RANZCOG GPS Vasa Praevia).
source_refs: RANZCOG GPS Vasa Praevia

options.text: Category 1 caesarean section for foetal compromise consistent with ruptured vasa praevia
options.rationale: Painless PV bleeding immediately after SROM in a woman with known velamentous insertion and bilobed placenta and rapid foetal deterioration is ruptured vasa praevia; foetal blood loss is catastrophic within minutes and only category 1 caesarean can save the compromised twin (Source: RANZCOG GPS Vasa Praevia).
source_refs: RANZCOG GPS Vasa Praevia

options.text: Administer intramuscular betamethasone 11.4 mg and defer delivery for at least 24 hours for lung maturation
options.rationale: Steroid maturation cannot be waited out in acute vasa praevia with foetal compromise; the diagnosis-to-birth interval determines survival and delay is not an option (Source: RANZCOG GPS Vasa Praevia).
source_refs: RANZCOG GPS Vasa Praevia

options.text: Perform digital vaginal examination to determine cervical dilatation before deciding on mode of delivery
options.rationale: Digital examination through the potentially exposed foetal vessel can worsen haemorrhage; the priority is immediate delivery, not further cervical examination, and prior speculum has already confirmed the bleeding pattern (Source: RANZCOG GPS Vasa Praevia).
source_refs: RANZCOG GPS Vasa Praevia

explanation.summary: Vasa praevia is unprotected foetal vessels crossing the internal cervical os, most often with velamentous cord insertion or bilobed or succenturiate placenta. IVF pregnancies and multiple gestations are additional risk factors. Painless PV bleeding immediately after rupture of membranes with rapid foetal deterioration is vasa praevia until proven otherwise. Foetal blood volume is small (about 250 mL at term) so exsanguination is minutes; category 1 caesarean is the only rescue and antenatal identification of vasa praevia should have prompted elective caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks before SROM.
key_points: Painless PV bleed immediately after SROM with foetal decelerations is vasa praevia
Category 1 caesarean is the only intervention that rescues the foetus in ruptured vasa praevia
Antenatal Doppler identification of vasa praevia mandates elective caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks
explanation.pearls: Placental abruption bleeds maternal blood and hurts; ruptured vasa praevia bleeds foetal blood and is painless with immediate foetal collapse.
